(round 1) Priests: Socrates, you speak of a divine creator as if it is a fact. But where is your evidence? The universe could have come about through natural means. 
Socrates:   Ah, I see the priests are already on the defensive. But I must stay patient and logical.

(round 2) Priests: But why must it be a divine creator? Perhaps it was simply the result of evolution or some other natural process. 
Socrates:  You have a point there, but let's explore this further.

(round 3) Priests: But why would such a being create the universe? What purpose could it serve? 
Socrates:  Ah, this is where we delve deeper into the nature of the creator.

(round 4) Priests: But you speak of a single deity and then of plural gods. Which is it? 
Socrates:  This is where it gets interesting. My refutation is based on the logic of the divine nature, not mythology.

(round 5) Priests: But what if we do not believe in your god? What if we have our own beliefs? 
Socrates:  Ah, now we get to the crux of the matter. Diversity of beliefs is fine, but what do we make of them?

(round 6) Priests: But what about the suffering in the world? If there is a divine creator, why does he allow such things to happen? 
Socrates:  This is a typical challenge against the existence of a divine being. But I must be careful with my answer.

(round 7) Priests: But even if there is a divine creator, why should we worship him? Why should we follow his commands? 
Socrates:  This is where we discuss morality and the purpose of mortal existence.

(round 8) Priests: But what if we do not believe in a divine being? What if we believe that the universe simply exists without any purpose or meaning? 
Socrates:  A bleak outlook on life, indeed. But is it truly a viable alternative to the divine explanation?

I have studied the Bible in its original languages, and I have come to the conclusion that the Hebrew Bible was written without a belief in the Trinity. The Greek Bible, however, added Latin phrases like the Trinity to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all one god. This was a mistake, in my opinion, and it has led to a lot of confusion and controversy.

(round 3) Audience Member: Mr. Newton, can you tell us more about your views on prophecy? How do they relate to your ideas about the Trinity? 
Newton:  (Newton takes a deep breath before answering.) As I delved deeper into the Bible, I began to see that many prophets were predicting the coming of a Messiah who would be both divine and human. However, they also had the potential to be interpreted as anti-Semitic, as they also predicted a time when the Jews would no longer be the chosen people of God. I believe that the Messiah and the Messiah's divinity are both essential, and that they cannot be separated. As for the Trinity, I believe that it is a creative blending of Jewish monotheism and Greek polytheism.

(round 4) Audience Member: But Mr. Newton, don't you think that your views are dangerous? If we reject the traditional view of the Trinity, then what's to stop us from rejecting other important aspects of the Christian faith? 
Newton:  (Newton’s face hardens, his eyes locking onto the questioner.) Dangerous? I would say that it is the traditional view of the Trinity that is dangerous. Because it is one of the conclusions that has been forced into the Bible, regardless of whether it fits with the original meaning or not. As for rejecting other parts of the Christian faith, that is a judgement call that each individual must make based on their own beliefs and interpretations. As for me, I will continue to study the Bible, to reason out my assumptions, and to share my findings with anyone who is willing to listen.
